content: To strengthen, integrate, and utilize information systems effectively, it is essential to establish a standardized set of national HIV indicators. These should be selected from the 18 key indicators outlined in the guidelines, taking into account the country’s progress in transitioning to the treat all approach. Any additional indicators must be chosen from the 2015 Consolidated Strategic Information Guidelines and should be strongly justified for their inclusion. For HIV patient monitoring and case surveillance, the generic tools and recommendations provided in the WHO Consolidated Guidelines on person-centered HIV patient monitoring and case surveillance should be adopted and tailored to the specific needs of each country and program. To update and standardize minimum datasets and tools, both paper-based and electronic systems should be revised. This includes updating core paper-based tools such as HIV patient cards, antiretroviral therapy (ART) registers, and cross-sectional and cohort reports. ART community monitoring tools, transfer/referral forms, patient-held cards, and appointment books should also be developed or updated as needed. Additionally, HIV data elements in maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH), tuberculosis (TB), and other relevant program monitoring tools should be revised. Electronic medical record systems, registers, and reporting systems must also be updated. A tiered approach should be adopted to determine when and how data from paper tools will be entered electronically, based on available resources and the specific site or setting. Harmonization of systems across program areas is crucial. HIV data elements, patient monitoring tools, and indicators should be standardized across facilities and programs, including TB and MNCH services. HIV patient cards and ART registers should be used at TB and MNCH sites. Service delivery should be integrated at the facility level, and HIV data should be incorporated into the Health Management Information System (HMIS). Collaboration with other national programs and external institutions is also necessary. To improve and sustain programs, quality data collected through key indicators should be analyzed, utilized, and fed back into the system. Periodic reviews (every six months or annually) of patient monitoring data should be conducted to assess data quality and gather additional key indicators. National and global reporting can be enhanced by simplifying disaggregation categories, standardizing reporting forms and tally tools, and establishing regular feedback loops. Patient monitoring, supervision, mentoring, and quality of care should be improved. Lay health workers should be allowed to collect and report data to reduce the burden on clinical staff. Available data should be used to create dashboards and other tools to identify gaps in care quality, which can then be addressed through routine analysis and periodic reviews. Unique patient identifiers should be assigned or developed, and patient appointment systems or linked pharmacy and clinical records should be used to identify and follow up with patients who are missing. Patient-held cards or passports and transfer/referral forms should be utilized to facilitate tracking of patients between service delivery points. Short-, medium-, and long-term plans for the patient monitoring system should be developed, incorporating strategic planning and policy documents, such as those from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria. A three-tiered patient monitoring system should include paper-based registers, electronic registers, and networked online systems. Essential elements for this system include proper folder flow and filing systems, standardized clinical stationery and reporting forms, protected time for data transcription, sufficient workspace for data capture, and access to electricity. Additionally, computers, printers, uninterruptible power supplies (UPS), memory storage devices, and staff with computer skills are necessary. A basic IT strategy should be in place to prevent computer viruses, send updates, and manage software versions. For networked systems, stable internet connections, network points within facilities, a central network team, and IT technicians with responsive turnaround times are required.
